interest: Shows Japan's 1932 banking crisis and Manchuria-driven deficit spending, per Feis's analysis, and a cable-cost-cutting instruction.
overview: Docket (April 1932): Neville reports Japan's banks held 9.46 billion yen in troubled loans amid deficits from the China campaign; Feis warns of inflationary financing and rural collapse; State also orders cheaper mail reporting over cable.

people.name: Edwin L. Neville
people.role: Counselor of Embassy / Chargé d'Affaires ad interim in Tokyo

subfiles.about: A telegraphic report detailing Japan's outstanding bank loans, bad debts, asset depreciation, and government budget deficits stemming from military operations in China.
subfiles.summary: Neville details Japan's 9.46 billion yen in bank loans, with collapsed land-mortgage values and deficit spending for the China campaign funded without foreign borrowing.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 107 from Neville (Tokyo) on Japanese Bank Loans and Government Finance

subfiles.about: A telegraphic instruction from the State Department directing the Tokyo Embassy to send subsequent economic reports by mail rather than cable to reduce expenses.
subfiles.summary: Carter instructs Tokyo to report economic data by mail rather than costly telegraph.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 86 from Acting Secretary Carter to American Embassy, Tokyo

subfiles.about: An internal Department of State memorandum analyzing Japan's growing revenue deficit, central bank credit inflation, agricultural crisis, and Manchurian financial commitments.
subfiles.summary: Feis warns Japan's deficits are financed by banking inflation, worsened by depressed silk prices and the cost of occupying Manchuria.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Herbert Feis on Japanese Deficit, Inflation, and Manchurian Finances
subfiles.to: Department of State / Office of the Economic Adviser
